summary:
H.J. Res. 153, introduced in the 119th Congress (2d Session) by Ms. Velazquez and referred to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, is a joint resolution invoking Congress's war powers to direct the removal of United States Armed Forces from unauthorized hostilities within or against the Republic of Cuba.

Section 1 sets forth findings, including: that Congress holds the sole power to declare war under Article I, Section 8, Clause 11; that the President bears constitutional responsibility to defend the United States and its personnel; that Congress has neither declared war against Cuba nor enacted a specific statutory authorization for the use of military force there; and that use of force within or against Cuba—expressly including use of the Coast Guard and other Armed Forces components to conduct a blockade or quarantine of Cuba—constitutes introduction of Armed Forces into hostilities within the meaning of section 4(a) of the War Powers Resolution (50 U.S.C. 1543(a)). The findings further recite that section 1013 of the Department of State Authorization Act, Fiscal Years 1984 and 1985 (50 U.S.C. 1546a) subjects such removal resolutions to the expedited procedures of section 601(b) of the International Security Assistance and Arms Export Control Act of 1976 (Pub. L. 94-329).

Section 2(a) contains the operative directive. Pursuant to 50 U.S.C. 1546a and in accordance with section 601(b) of the International Security Assistance and Arms Export Control Act of 1976, Congress directs the President to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless such hostilities are explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force. The resolution operates as a concurrent exercise of the War Powers Resolution's removal mechanism rather than as an amendment to any existing statute; it neither authorizes nor appropriates funds.

Section 2(b) provides a rule of construction stating that nothing in the section may be construed to prevent the United States from defending itself against an armed attack or the threat of an imminent armed attack, or from the lawful execution of counternarcotics operations.

The resolution does not specify a numerical deadline for removal, an effective date, a sunset, or an enforcement mechanism beyond the statutory directive and the incorporated expedited-procedure framework. Its legal force derives from the privileged consideration procedures referenced in 50 U.S.C. 1546a and section 601(b) of Pub. L. 94-329.
